transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-18 14:00 UTC | Duration ~75m | Recorded by Fireflies
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Omar Patel (Redwood Solutions), Marta Ruiz (Vertex Labs, Search Eng), Ben Cho (Vertex Labs, ML Infra), Leah Grant (CTO), Ibrahim Noor (SRE)
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Today we want to focus on the reranker pipeline economics — specifically how embedding dimension and batching tie into latency SLOs and per-query cost. Priya will walk through the runtime profiles.
[00:28] Priya: Hi all — quick context question: what SLOs are you targeting end-to-end for search rerank? Is this 200ms or tighter?
[00:38] Marta: We want 150ms p95 for the production channel, but new verticals might push to 100ms. Throughput target is 300 QPS peak.
[00:48] Ben: Also worth noting token counts on our side — queries are short but reranker uses context snippets that average 512 tokens.
[00:58] Priya: Great, that helps. High-level split: you have an embedding generation stage per candidate set, an ANN index lookup (HNSW) to get top-K, and then a neural reranker that runs on the top 20 results. We typically see the reranker dominate GPU latency when it's not batched.
[01:20] Omar: Two quick clarifiers — when we say embedding dimension, are we talking about the vectors used for ANN retrieval (64/128/256/512) or the reranker model input embeddings?
[01:32] Priya: Good call — mostly retrieval vectors. The reranker uses a separate cross-encoder, smaller, usually FP16. But retrieval dim affects index size and ANN CPU/GPU cost.
[01:44] Marta: We've been experimenting with 512-dim for recall, but storage and flight costs on our on-prem HSM nodes exploded. That's why we asked for the cost deep dive.
[01:55] Priya: Right. Quick rule of thumb: doubling dims ~ doubles index memory and increases nearest neighbor compute roughly linearly. But for some models, recall gains saturate after 128 or 256 depending on dataset.
[02:10] Ben: On our infra we saw RAM on HNSW jump by 3x moving 128->512 due to graph degree and stored payloads. Does Redwood have hosted optimizations for that?
[02:20] Jordan: In hosted we shard the index across GPUs and have options to store compressed vectors using 8-bit product quantization; for Dedicated/Private we recommend quantized index formats or lower dims for memory-limited nodes.
[02:34] Priya: For the embedding generator itself, running FP16 int8-quantized encoders reduces GPU memory and increases batch capacity, but careful: int8 can shift nearest neighbor geometry slightly, so you should validate with your gold set.
[02:50] Ibrahim: How does KV cache fit here? We thought prefix caching would help reranker latency because many workflows reuse the same context.
[02:58] Priya: KV cache is most effective for autoregressive generation where tokens reuse previous KV. For reranking flows, if you can cache candidate embeddings or reranker intermediate tensors, you'll see hit-rate benefits. In practice, caching top-K embedding results per query fingerprint gives big wins for repeated queries.
[03:16] Marta: Our tail workload has a long tail of unique queries, so cache hit rate is maybe 15–20% right now.
[03:24] Priya: In that case, batching becomes the main lever. If you can tolerate a small p50 increase to reduce cost, batch sizes of 4–8 for the reranker often hit a sweet spot: improves GPU throughput and amortizes kernel launch, but p99 may suffer if you wait for large batches.
[03:43] Ben: Do you have numbers for p50/p95/p99 change vs batch size?
[03:48] Priya: We ran a similar workload: batch=1 p50=18ms p95=120ms p99=320ms (per-reranker call, FP16, 20 top-K). batch=4 p50=9ms p95=45ms p99=210ms. batch=8 p50=7ms p95=38ms p99=260ms — you see p95 improves then p99 can regress because of stragglers waiting for batch fill. These are anecdotal but we will reproduce against your QPS.
[04:18] Jordan: Important note: your latency SLO is p95 150ms end-to-end. If reranker p95 is 45ms and retrieval+index+network adds 60–80ms, you can be close. But for p99 we need fallbacks — e.g., degrade to a cheaper reranker or cached result.
[04:34] Leah: What's the cost impact of moving from 128->256 dims for us at 300 QPS? Ballpark per 100k queries?
[04:43] Jordan: Quick back-of-envelope: index storage and CPU cost mostly scale with dims. If 128 dim index cost is X, 256 is ~1.8–2.1X depending on PQ compression. For GPU inference cost, embedding generator time scales modestly; reranker cost is unaffected by retrieval dim. We'll produce a detailed pricing worksheet showing cost per 100k queries across dims and batch configs.
[05:05] Marta: Can quantization break recall in subtle ways? We saw small drops in nDCG at 512->int8 for one model.
[05:12] Priya: Yes, quantization introduces distortions. For embedding vectors we recommend product quantization (PQ) with 8-bit subquantizers and validating against your evaluation set. For cross-encoder rerankers, int8 activation quantization can change ranking; typically we keep reranker FP16 and quantize retrieval encoder and ANN.
[05:30] Ben: For Private/VPC deployment, any differences in KV cache behavior? We plan to keep index in a private subnet and use a dedicated pool of inference nodes.
[05:39] Priya: Behavior is the same functionally, but latency to the index can increase if the network path is longer. We recommend colocating ANN index and reranker on the same node or use a low-latency fabric. Also warmup strategies: keep a small steady-state worker pool to avoid cold-start p99 spikes.
[05:56] Ibrahim: Related to warmup — what's the recommended autoscale policy to avoid p99 spikes but still control cost?
[06:04] Jordan: A hybrid: baseline reserved workers for steady QPS plus scaled workers for burst. Use fast scale-up with queue-based thresholds and slow scale-down cooldown to avoid thrash. Redwood Dedicated supports pre-warmed burst instances.
[06:18] Marta: Can you run a benchmark where we try dims 64/128/256 with batching 1/4/8 and both PQ and raw vectors? We'll need p50/p95/p99, throughput, RAM per shard, and cost estimate.
[06:29] Priya: Yes — that's exactly what we'll run. We'll also capture KV cache hit/no-hit permutations. If you can provide the 10k queries and gold labels, we will compute nDCG/regression vs each config.
[06:40] Ben: On indexing, what's the recommended HNSW degree and efConstruction for these dims? We currently use defaults and memory looks high.
[06:48] Priya: Lowering M (degree) reduces memory and may slightly affect recall. For high-dim vectors, tuning efConstruction and M per shard is critical. We'll include suggested starting points in the deliverable.
[06:59] Jordan: Quick recap of next actions: Redwood runs benchmarks, sends pricing worksheet, and shares PQ caveats doc. Vertex provides dataset + SLOs. Follow-up sync to review results.
[07:12] Marta: Sounds good. Appreciate the practical numbers.
[07:18] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll send calendar invite for the results review.
[75:00] End of recording — casual wrap-up and off-record action assignments.
